title: Teens and the “3 p.m. to 3 a.m.” Problem
author: Rick Hess
summary: Rick Hess interviews Mike Goldstein, founder of Match Education and co-founder of the Center for Teen Flourishing, an R&D lab on how teens spend the hours between leaving school and going to bed. Goldstein cites data showing declines in sleep, pleasure reading and face-to-face hangout time, and a minority of teens who are flourishing. He defines flourishing as spending 15 hours a week outside school in real-life activities such as sports, music, work or friends, and describes "languishing" teens who spend hours alone with a screen. He proposes a state competition to raise flourishing and a National Assessment of Flourishing and Participation, and suggests schools use advisory periods or hire recent graduates to connect teens to existing clubs and community groups. He largely endorses Haidt but frames the culprit as total recreational screen time. His advice to educators is to ask five teens what they do hour by hour and help them find one real-life activity.
points: Goldstein reframes teen wellbeing around the 3 p.m. to 3 a.m. hours, where isolation, scrolling and anxiety have risen while real-life activity has fallen.
His working definition of flourishing, 15 hours a week of real-life activities, is admittedly arbitrary but offered as a usable target, like 10,000 steps.
He argues the problem is total recreational screen time crowding out sleep, exercise and friendships, not social media alone.
Schools can act as "adult sherpas," using advisory periods or dedicated staff to link languishing students to open slots in teams, clubs and community groups.
He proposes measuring the problem, via a national assessment of flourishing and participation, so that states compete on it as they do on NAEP scores.
quotes: The Center for Teen Flourishing is an R&D lab focused on understanding how teens are doing in the 3 p.m. to 3 a.m. hours—from when kids get out of school to when they go to bed.
We define flourishing teens as those who spend 15 hours per week outside of school engaged in “real life” activities like sports, music, working, or socializing with friends.
Often, they get home from school, close their bedroom door, and spend six or seven hours alone with a screen.

The good news is that many communities have lots of unused capacity—open slots on school sports teams and clubs or community and religious organizations looking for more teens. They’re just missing the adult sherpas who can nudge the kids to get involved.
We think social psychologist Jonathan Haidt generally gets the story right, but we’d reframe the culprit as total recreational screen time, not just social media.
Using screens six-plus hours a day crowds out the “real-life good stuff” like sleep, exercise, and friendships.
Pick five teens you’re close with. Ask them what they do, hour by hour, on weekdays after school and on weekends.
